name: SOC 2
scopeSummary: Covers the service organization's system boundary and the Trust Services Criteria selected (security is required; availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy are optional).
keyObligationsSummary: Management defines the system, asserts control design and operation, and engages a licensed CPA firm to examine controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. Type 1 reports on design at a point in time; Type 2 reports on operating effectiveness over a period, commonly 3 to 12 months. The output is an attestation report rather than a pass/fail certificate.

name: SOC 1
scopeSummary: Covers controls relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) for the described service.
keyObligationsSummary: Management describes the system and control objectives relevant to financial reporting and a CPA firm examines them under SSAE 18 (AT-C 320). Reports are issued as Type 1 (design) or Type 2 (design and operating effectiveness). User auditors rely on the report during their customers' financial audits.

name: SOC 3
alsoKnownAs: Trust Services Report for General Use
scopeSummary: Same scope as the underlying SOC 2 examination, presented as a general-use summary report.
keyObligationsSummary: A SOC 3 report is a general-use version of a SOC 2 Type 2 engagement without the detailed test procedures and results. It can be published or posted publicly, unlike restricted-use SOC 2 reports. It does not replace a SOC 2 report in security reviews.

name: ISO/IEC 27001
scopeSummary: Applies to the information security management system (ISMS) scope the organization defines, including people, processes and technology inside that boundary.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a documented ISMS with leadership commitment, risk assessment and treatment, a Statement of Applicability covering Annex A controls, internal audit and management review. Certification is issued by an accredited certification body after Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits. Surveillance audits occur annually with full recertification every three years.

name: ISO/IEC 27002
scopeSummary: Guidance standard covering the information security controls referenced by ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides implementation guidance and purpose statements for each control rather than certifiable management-system requirements. Organizations are not certified against ISO/IEC 27002 itself. It is commonly used to justify Statement of Applicability decisions.

name: ISO/IEC 27017
scopeSummary: Covers cloud service provider and cloud service customer responsibilities for information security in cloud environments.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides cloud-specific implementation guidance for ISO/IEC 27002 controls plus additional cloud controls, including shared responsibility, virtual environment segregation and administrative operations. It is usually assessed as an extension to an ISO/IEC 27001 certification scope.

name: ISO/IEC 27018
scopeSummary: Covers PII protection controls for public cloud service providers processing personal data on behalf of customers.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides a code of practice with additional controls and guidance for cloud processors, including transparency about subprocessors, data location and return or deletion of data. It is typically certified as an extension to an ISO/IEC 27001 scope. It does not by itself establish legal compliance with privacy laws.

name: ISO/IEC 27701
scopeSummary: Covers a Privacy Information Management System (PIMS) for organizations acting as PII controllers, PII processors or both, within a defined ISMS scope.
keyObligationsSummary: Extends ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 with privacy-specific requirements and controls for controllers and processors, including purpose limitation, data subject rights handling, records of processing and transfer transparency. Certification requires an existing or concurrent ISO/IEC 27001 certification. Annexes map controls to GDPR articles, which supports but does not prove legal compliance.

name: ISO/IEC 42001
scopeSummary: Covers an AI management system (AIMS) for the AI systems and roles inside the declared scope, for providers and users of AI.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires an AI management system with AI risk assessment, AI system impact assessment, defined roles across the AI lifecycle, and controls for data, model and third-party management. It is certifiable by accredited certification bodies. It is a governance standard and does not itself demonstrate conformity with AI legislation.

name: ISO 22301
scopeSummary: Covers a business continuity management system (BCMS) for the products, services and sites in the declared scope.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires business impact analysis, risk assessment, continuity strategies, documented plans, and exercising and testing of those plans. Certification is available from accredited bodies. Many buyers accept BCMS evidence without full certification.

name: ISO 9001
scopeSummary: Covers a quality management system (QMS) for the products and services in the declared scope.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a process-based QMS with customer focus, documented processes, competence management, nonconformity and corrective action handling, internal audit and management review. Certification is issued by accredited certification bodies. It addresses quality management, not information security.

name: ISO 14001
scopeSummary: Covers an environmental management system (EMS) for the activities, products and services in the declared scope.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires identification of environmental aspects and compliance obligations, environmental objectives, operational controls, emergency preparedness, internal audit and management review. Certification is issued by accredited certification bodies. It manages environmental performance rather than information security or privacy.

name: ISO 13485
scopeSummary: Covers a quality management system for organizations involved in one or more stages of the medical device lifecycle.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a documented quality management system with design and development controls, risk management across the lifecycle, supplier controls, traceability, complaint handling and regulatory reporting processes. Certification supports regulatory approvals such as EU MDR conformity assessment and is widely expected by notified bodies. It is quality-system focused and does not replace product conformity assessment.

name: ISO/IEC 20000-1
scopeSummary: Covers a service management system (SMS) for the services in the declared scope.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a documented service management system with service planning, service level management, incident, problem and change management, and continual improvement. Certification is available from accredited bodies. It complements but does not replace security certifications.

name: ISO 31000
scopeSummary: Guidance for managing risk across any organization type, size or sector; not scoped to a specific system.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides principles, a framework and a process for risk management including identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment, monitoring and communication. It is guidance only and is not certifiable. It is commonly referenced to justify risk methodology in ISO 27001 or SOC 2 programs.

name: ISA/IEC 62443
alsoKnownAs: industrial automation and control systems security
scopeSummary: Covers industrial automation and control systems organized into zones and conduits, with roles for asset owners, integrators and product suppliers.
keyObligationsSummary: Defines security program requirements for asset owners, security requirements for integration service providers, secure product development lifecycle requirements for suppliers, and technical system and component security requirements. Security levels 1 to 4 express the strength of protection required for each zone. Certification schemes such as ISASecure and IECEE assess products, processes and systems.

name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
scopeSummary: Voluntary framework applicable to organizations of any size or sector; scope is defined by the organization.
keyObligationsSummary: Organizes cybersecurity outcomes into functions and categories that organizations use to assess current and target profiles. Version 2.0, published in 2024, added the Govern function alongside Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. It is outcome-based, so implementation is chosen by the organization and there is no certification.

name: NIST SP 800-53
scopeSummary: Applies to federal information systems and organizations, and to non-federal systems where adopted by contract or program such as FedRAMP.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides a catalog of security and privacy controls with low, moderate and high baselines selected by system categorization. Control selection is paired with assessment procedures in SP 800-53A. FedRAMP and FISMA programs use tailored baselines drawn from this catalog.

name: NIST SP 800-171
scopeSummary: Applies to CUI in nonfederal systems and organizations, scoped to the environment where CUI is handled.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires implementation of security requirements for protecting CUI, a system security plan and plans of action for gaps. DFARS 252.204-7012 obliges many defense contractors to implement it and report scores, and CMMC assessments verify it. Revision 3 restructured the requirement families and tailoring approach.

name: NIST SP 800-172
scopeSummary: Applies as a supplement to SP 800-171 for selected systems and components identified by the contracting agency.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides enhanced security requirements aimed at advanced persistent threats, including penetration-resistant architecture and cyber resiliency measures. Requirements apply only when specified by the federal agency or contract. It is used for CMMC Level 3 assessment content.

name: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework
scopeSummary: Covers secure software development practices across the software development lifecycle for the producer's software.
keyObligationsSummary: Describes practices grouped into preparing the organization, protecting software, producing well-secured software and responding to vulnerabilities. It is referenced by U.S. federal secure software development attestation requirements for software sold to agencies. It is guidance rather than a certification.

name: NIST Privacy Framework
scopeSummary: Voluntary framework for managing privacy risk arising from data processing; scope is defined by the organization.
keyObligationsSummary: Organizes privacy outcomes into functions and categories that organizations use to build current and target profiles alongside the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. It is voluntary, non-certifiable and technology-neutral. Tennessee's privacy statute provides an affirmative defense for programs that reasonably conform to it.

name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
scopeSummary: Voluntary framework for AI risks across the AI lifecycle; scope is set by the organization and AI use cases.
keyObligationsSummary: Organizes AI risk management into the Govern, Map, Measure and Manage functions with characteristics of trustworthy AI. It is voluntary and not certifiable, and is often paired with the companion Playbook and generative AI profile. Many buyers use it as the structure for AI governance evidence.

name: CIS Critical Security Controls
scopeSummary: Applies to the enterprise's assets, accounts, data and networks; implementation groups scale scope by organization size and risk.
keyObligationsSummary: Defines prioritized safeguards across 18 controls, grouped into Implementation Groups IG1 to IG3. IG1 is described as essential cyber hygiene for smaller organizations. The controls are voluntary, mapped to other frameworks, and not certifiable, though CIS offers self-assessment tooling.

name: CIS Benchmarks
scopeSummary: Covers secure configuration baselines for specific technologies and versions rather than an organization-wide management system.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides consensus-developed configuration recommendations with rationale, audit and remediation steps, generally organized into Level 1 and Level 2 profiles. Organizations select applicable benchmarks, document deviations and monitor drift, often using automated assessment tooling. There is no certification, though CIS Hardened Images and CIS-CAT support implementation and measurement.

name: CSA STAR
scopeSummary: Covers the cloud service offering assessed against the Cloud Controls Matrix, at the level of assurance chosen.
keyObligationsSummary: Providers document controls against the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix and CAIQ and may publish results in the STAR Registry. Level 1 is self-assessment, Level 2 is third-party certification or attestation combined with ISO 27001 or SOC 2, and continuous monitoring options exist. Listing serves as a reusable trust artifact for cloud diligence.

name: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard
scopeSummary: Covers application-level security requirements for the application or API under review.
keyObligationsSummary: Provides a catalog of verification requirements across levels of rigor that teams use for secure design, development and testing. It is a community standard with no formal certification body. It is often referenced in penetration test scopes and secure development policies.

name: PCI DSS
alsoKnownAs: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
scopeSummary: Covers the cardholder data environment, connected systems and any people and processes with access to account data.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires implementation of technical and operational requirements across network security, data protection, vulnerability management, access control, monitoring and policy. Validation depends on merchant or service provider level and channel, using a Self-Assessment Questionnaire with an Attestation of Compliance or a Report on Compliance by a QSA. Version 4.0.1 is the current standard, with customized approach options and additional authentication and script-management requirements.

name: PCI Software Security Framework
scopeSummary: Covers payment software products under the Secure Software Standard and vendor development processes under the Secure Software Lifecycle Standard.
keyObligationsSummary: The Secure Software Standard sets security objectives for payment software including sensitive data protection, attack detection and secure updates, validated by a qualified assessor. The Secure SLC Standard validates the vendor's development lifecycle so qualifying changes can be released without full revalidation. Validated products and vendors are listed by the PCI Security Standards Council and the framework replaced PA-DSS.

name: PCI 3DS Core Security Standard
scopeSummary: Covers the 3DS environment and the systems, processes and personnel performing 3DS functions.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires baseline security controls plus 3DS-specific requirements covering key management, transaction data protection and segregation of the 3DS environment. Assessment is performed by a qualified 3DS assessor, resulting in a Report on Compliance and Attestation of Compliance. It is generally applied in addition to, not instead of, PCI DSS where cardholder data is present.

name: SWIFT Customer Security Programme
scopeSummary: Covers the user's Swift-related infrastructure and the architecture type declared, from full local footprint to fully outsourced connectivity.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires implementation of the Customer Security Controls Framework, comprising mandatory and advisory controls scoped by architecture type. Users must submit an annual attestation through the KYC-Security Attestation application, supported by an independent assessment, either internal or external. Non-compliance can be reported to supervisors and to counterparties.

name: HITRUST CSF
scopeSummary: Covers the in-scope systems and facilities assessed against the HITRUST CSF at the selected assessment type.
keyObligationsSummary: Organizations scope requirements through the HITRUST MyCSF platform, implement the mapped control requirements and undergo validation by an authorized external assessor before HITRUST issues certification. Assessment types include the e1 essentials, i1 implemented and r2 risk-based options with differing rigor and validity. The CSF maps to multiple authoritative sources including HIPAA, NIST and ISO.

name: FedRAMP
alsoKnownAs: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program
scopeSummary: Covers the cloud service offering boundary and its supporting infrastructure at the authorized impact level.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires implementation of NIST SP 800-53 baselines tailored by FedRAMP, assessment by an accredited third-party assessment organization, and authorization by an agency or the FedRAMP program. Authorized offerings must maintain continuous monitoring with monthly deliverables and annual assessments. Impact levels are Low, Moderate and High, with FedRAMP Tailored options for lower-risk services.

name: GovRAMP
alsoKnownAs: State Risk and Authorization Management Program
scopeSummary: Covers the cloud offering boundary assessed at the required impact level for participating state and local governments.
keyObligationsSummary: Uses NIST SP 800-53 based security requirements verified by a third-party assessment organization, with progressive statuses leading to Authorized. Verified offerings are listed for participating governments and require continuous monitoring. Requirements closely mirror FedRAMP, and FedRAMP packages can often be reciprocally recognized.

name: TX-RAMP
alsoKnownAs: Texas Risk and Authorization Management Program
scopeSummary: Covers cloud computing services that process, store or transmit Texas state agency data, categorized by impact level.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires certification at Level 1 for higher-impact data or Level 2 for lower-impact data, based on evidence such as a StateRAMP or FedRAMP authorization, or a Texas-specific assessment package. State agencies may not enter or renew contracts for cloud services that lack the required status. The Department of Information Resources manages the program and publishes certified services.

name: Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification
scopeSummary: Applies to the contractor systems that process, store or transmit FCI or CUI, scoped to the assessment boundary.
keyObligationsSummary: Establishes three levels: Level 1 self-assessment for FCI based on FAR 52.204-21, Level 2 based on NIST SP 800-171 (self or C3PAO certification assessment), and Level 3 adding selected NIST SP 800-172 requirements assessed by DCMA DIBCAC. Contractors must post results and affirmations in SPRS. Required levels are set in solicitations under the DoD acquisition rule.

name: Federal Information Security Modernization Act
issuingBody: US Congress; overseen by CISA and OMB
scopeSummary: Applies to federal information and information systems, including contractor systems used or operated for an agency.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires agencies to run an information security program with system categorization under FIPS 199, control selection from NIST SP 800-53, assessment and authorization, and continuous monitoring. Agencies report annually to OMB and Congress. Contractors inherit requirements through contract terms.

name: DFARS 252.204-7012
scopeSummary: Applies to covered contractor information systems that process, store or transmit covered defense information.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires implementation of NIST SP 800-171 security requirements, rapid reporting of cyber incidents to DoD within 72 hours, media preservation, malicious software submission and flow-down to subcontractors. Cloud services used to store covered defense information must generally meet DoD cloud security requirements. It is imposed through the contract clause.

name: International Traffic in Arms Regulations
scopeSummary: Applies to defense articles and technical data on the USML, including software and technical data shared with foreign persons, wherever located.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires registration with the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls for manufacturers, exporters and brokers, licensing or use of exemptions for exports and re-exports, and controls preventing deemed exports to foreign persons. Recordkeeping and access controls over technical data are required, including for cloud environments. Compliance programs commonly include personnel screening and encryption practices.

name: Export Administration Regulations
issuingBody: US Bureau of Industry and Security
scopeSummary: Applies to items subject to the EAR, including those on the Commerce Control List and EAR99 items, and to deemed exports of technology to foreign nationals.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires classification of items, determination of license requirements by country, end user and end use, screening against restricted party lists, and recordkeeping. Encryption software has specific classification and reporting rules. License exceptions may apply but must be documented.

name: Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act
scopeSummary: Covers ICT developed, procured, maintained or used by federal agencies, including software, websites, documents and hardware.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires ICT to conform to the Revised 508 Standards, which incorporate WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA success criteria for web and non-web content plus hardware and support documentation requirements. Vendors typically document conformance in an Accessibility Conformance Report based on the VPAT template. Agencies must assess and report on accessibility, and procurement can be challenged for non-conforming ICT.

name: Americans with Disabilities Act
alsoKnownAs: ADA Title II web accessibility rule
scopeSummary: Covers discrimination on the basis of disability, applied by courts and DOJ rulemaking to websites, mobile apps and other digital services.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires that goods, services and programs be accessible to people with disabilities, including effective communication and reasonable modifications. The 2024 Title II rule requires state and local government web content and mobile apps to conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, with compliance dates in 2026 and 2027 depending on entity size. For private businesses under Title III there is no codified technical standard, so WCAG conformance is the prevailing benchmark used in litigation and settlements.

name: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
scopeSummary: Covers web content, including web applications, documents and, through WCAG2ICT guidance, non-web software and content.
keyObligationsSummary: Organizes accessibility requirements under the perceivable, operable, understandable and robust principles, with testable success criteria at conformance levels A, AA and AAA. Level AA is the common regulatory and contractual benchmark. Conformance is self-declared or evaluated by specialists, since there is no certification body.

name: UK G-Cloud Framework
scopeSummary: Covers services listed on the framework and the associated framework and call-off contract terms, not a security control set.
keyObligationsSummary: Suppliers apply during a framework iteration, submit service definitions, pricing and terms, and must keep listings accurate. Call-off contracts impose obligations that commonly include security, data protection, transparency and exit assistance, and buyers frequently require Cyber Essentials or equivalent assurance. Listings are only valid for the framework term, so re-application is needed for successor iterations.

name: Cyber Essentials
scopeSummary: Covers internet-facing infrastructure, devices, software and user accounts within the declared organizational scope.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires implementation of five technical control themes: firewalls, secure configuration, security update management, user access control and malware protection. Basic certification is a verified self-assessment; Cyber Essentials Plus adds hands-on technical verification by an assessor. Certification is valid for twelve months.

name: Infosec Registered Assessors Program
scopeSummary: Covers the system or service assessed against the Australian Government Information Security Manual controls at the relevant classification level.
keyObligationsSummary: An IRAP-endorsed assessor evaluates the system against the ISM controls and produces a security assessment report; the government entity then makes its own risk-based authorization decision. IRAP is an assessment process, not a certification issued by the ASD. Scope and classification level determine applicable controls.

name: ACSC Essential Eight
scopeSummary: Applies to the organization's internet-connected IT environment; maturity levels scale with threat sophistication.
keyObligationsSummary: Defines eight mitigation strategies including application control, patching applications and operating systems, configuring macro settings, user application hardening, restricting administrative privileges, multi-factor authentication and regular backups. Maturity Levels One to Three describe increasing rigor. Non-corporate Commonwealth entities are directed to implement it, and it is widely used commercially as a baseline.

name: BSI Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue
issuingBody: German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI)
scopeSummary: Covers the cloud service in scope against the BSI Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue.
keyObligationsSummary: Providers are assessed by an auditor against the C5 criteria and receive an attestation report based on ISAE 3000 style engagements, issued as Type 1 or Type 2. The catalogue includes basic and additional criteria plus mandatory environmental disclosures about jurisdiction and data location. German federal customers frequently require C5 attestation.

name: Esquema Nacional de Seguridad
scopeSummary: Covers information systems used to provide services to Spanish public administrations, categorized as basic, medium or high.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires system categorization, a risk analysis, a declaration or certification of conformity, and implementation of the security measures in Annex II appropriate to the category. Basic-category systems may use a self-declaration, while medium and high categories require certification by an accredited conformity assessment entity. Conformity must be published and maintained.

name: ISMAP
alsoKnownAs: Information system Security Management and Assessment Program
issuingBody: ISMAP Steering Committee (Digital Agency, METI, MIC)
scopeSummary: Covers the registered cloud service and its management, operational and technical controls, with a separate lighter track for low-risk services.
keyObligationsSummary: Providers implement the ISMAP control criteria, undergo an audit by an ISMAP-registered auditing firm, and apply for registration on the ISMAP cloud service list maintained by the steering committee. Government procurement is generally limited to registered services. Registration must be renewed through periodic audits and updated for significant changes.

name: ISMS-P (Korea)
alsoKnownAs: Personal Information and Information Security Management System
scopeSummary: Covers the certified management system scope, either ISMS for information security or ISMS-P which adds personal information protection.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires implementation of management system requirements and control items, an internal review, and certification audit by an authorized certification body under KISA and the PIPC. Certain service providers are legally required to obtain ISMS certification based on revenue and user thresholds. Certificates are valid for three years with annual follow-up audits.

name: Multi-Tier Cloud Security Singapore Standard
issuingBody: Infocomm Media Development Authority; Singapore Standards Council
scopeSummary: Covers the cloud service and supporting infrastructure certified at Level 1, 2 or 3 according to data sensitivity and business impact.
keyObligationsSummary: Providers implement the SS 584 controls for the target tier and are certified by an accredited certification body. Level 3 is aimed at regulated and high-impact workloads and includes the most extensive control set. Certification is accompanied by a self-disclosure schedule that customers use for due diligence.

name: TISAX
scopeSummary: Covers the sites and services in the declared assessment scope against the VDA ISA catalogue at the required assessment level.
keyObligationsSummary: Participants perform a VDA ISA self-assessment, undergo an audit by an accredited provider at the required assessment level, and share results through the ENX exchange rather than receiving a public certificate. Assessment objectives cover information security, prototype protection and data protection depending on scope. Labels are typically valid for three years.

name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule
scopeSummary: Applies to online collection, use and disclosure of personal information from children under 13, including through third-party services integrated into child-directed properties.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a clear online privacy notice, direct notice and verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children, and a means for parents to review or delete data and revoke consent. Operators must limit collection to what is reasonably necessary, retain data only as long as needed, and maintain reasonable security including vendor assurances. The amended COPPA Rule adds requirements such as a written children's data security program and separate consent for third-party disclosures including targeted advertising.

name: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act
scopeSummary: Applies to education records containing personally identifiable information about students held by covered schools and their designated school officials.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires parental or eligible-student consent before disclosing personally identifiable information from education records, unless an exception such as the school official exception applies. Vendors relying on that exception must use the data only for authorized purposes, remain under the school's direct control and not redisclose without authorization. Schools must provide annual notification of rights and allow inspection, review and amendment requests.

name: CAN-SPAM Act
scopeSummary: Applies to commercial electronic mail messages, with lighter rules for transactional or relationship messages, regardless of whether the list is opt-in.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires accurate header and sender information, non-deceptive subject lines, identification of the message as an advertisement where applicable, a valid physical postal address, and a clear opt-out mechanism. Opt-out requests must be honored within ten business days and the mechanism must remain functional for at least 30 days after sending. Senders remain responsible for compliance by affiliates and agents acting on their behalf.

name: Telephone Consumer Protection Act
scopeSummary: Applies to calls and texts using an automatic telephone dialing system or artificial or prerecorded voice, telemarketing to residential and wireless numbers, and unsolicited fax advertisements.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires prior express consent for many automated calls and texts, and prior express written consent for marketing calls and texts to wireless numbers and for artificial or prerecorded telemarketing calls. Callers must honor do-not-call requests, screen against the National Do Not Call Registry for telemarketing, provide identification and an opt-out mechanism, and observe calling-time restrictions. FCC rules also require revocation of consent to be honored promptly, generally within ten business days.

name: Fair Credit Reporting Act
scopeSummary: Applies to consumer reports used for credit, employment, insurance, tenancy and other permissible purposes, including background screening and some data analytics products.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires permissible purpose for obtaining consumer reports, disclosure and written authorization for employment screening, and pre-adverse and adverse action notices with a copy of the report and summary of rights. Consumer reporting agencies must follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy, investigate disputes and honor consumer file access rights. Furnishers must provide accurate information and investigate disputed items.

name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act
scopeSummary: Applies to biometric identifiers such as fingerprints, voiceprints, retina or iris scans and face geometry, and to biometric information derived from them.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a written, publicly available retention and destruction policy, informed written consent before collection, and a prohibition on selling or profiting from biometric data. Disclosure to third parties generally requires consent, and entities must store biometric data using the reasonable standard of care applicable to their industry. Illinois amended the statute in 2024 so that repeated collections of the same biometric from the same person generally give rise to a single violation.

name: Washington My Health My Data Act
issuingBody: Washington State Legislature; Washington Attorney General
scopeSummary: Applies to consumer health data, defined broadly to include information that identifies a consumer's past, present or future physical or mental health status, including inferences and precise location near health facilities.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a separate consumer health data privacy policy, opt-in consent for collection and sharing beyond what is necessary for a requested product or service, and separate valid authorization to sell such data. Consumers have rights to confirm, access, withdraw consent and delete their health data, including deletion by downstream recipients. Geofencing around in-person health service locations for advertising or data collection is prohibited.

name: NYC Local Law 144
alsoKnownAs: automated employment decision tools bias audit
issuingBody: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
scopeSummary: Covers automated employment decision tools used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decisions for NYC-based positions.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires an independent bias audit within one year before use, calculating selection or scoring rates and impact ratios by sex and race or ethnicity categories, with a public summary of results posted on the employer's website. Candidates and employees must receive at least ten business days' notice before use, including the job qualifications and characteristics assessed. Enforcement is by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

name: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act
scopeSummary: Covers AI analysis of applicant video interviews, including the notice, consent, sharing and deletion of those recordings.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires notifying applicants before the interview that AI may be used, explaining how the AI works and what characteristics it evaluates, and obtaining consent. Videos may be shared only with persons whose expertise is necessary to evaluate the applicant, and must be deleted, including backups, within 30 days of an applicant's deletion request. Employers that rely solely on AI to decide who advances to in-person interviews must collect and report race and ethnicity data annually to the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity.

name: California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by CPRA
issuingBody: California Privacy Protection Agency; California Attorney General
scopeSummary: Applies to personal information of California residents, including employees, job applicants and business contacts, with entity- and data-level exemptions such as HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires notices at collection and a comprehensive privacy policy, and support for rights to know, delete, correct, opt out of sale or sharing, limit use of sensitive personal information and non-discrimination. Businesses must honor opt-out preference signals such as Global Privacy Control, provide a Do Not Sell or Share link where applicable, and use compliant contracts with service providers, contractors and third parties. Risk assessments, cybersecurity audits and automated decision-making rules apply under CPPA regulations on a phased timeline.

name: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act
issuingBody: Virginia General Assembly; Virginia Attorney General
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Virginia residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Nonprofits and institutions of higher education are exempt.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on January 1, 2023. Consent is required before processing sensitive data, and data protection assessments are required for targeted advertising, sale, certain profiling and sensitive data processing.

name: Colorado Privacy Act
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Colorado residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Nonprofits are covered, unlike in several other states.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on July 1, 2023. Controllers must recognize universal opt-out mechanisms on the Attorney General's public list, obtain consent for sensitive data and for processing minors' data for targeted advertising, and complete data protection assessments for higher-risk processing.

name: Connecticut Data Privacy Act
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Connecticut residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Nonprofits and higher education institutions were exempt originally, and 2025 amendments broaden scope and tighten duties on a later effective date.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on July 1, 2023. Consent is required for sensitive data including consumer health data and for targeted advertising or sale involving minors, and data protection assessments are required for higher-risk processing.

name: Utah Consumer Privacy Act
issuingBody: Utah Legislature; Utah Division of Consumer Protection
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Utah residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Applies only to controllers or processors with annual revenue of 25 million US dollars or more.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on December 31, 2023. This law is comparatively light: there is no right to correct, no data protection assessment requirement, and sensitive data requires notice and an opportunity to opt out rather than opt-in consent.

name: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Texas residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Applicability is based on business size rather than consumer counts.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on July 1, 2024. Consent is required for sensitive data, controllers that sell sensitive or biometric data must post prescribed notices, and data protection assessments are required for higher-risk processing.

name: Oregon Consumer Privacy Act
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Oregon residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Nonprofits became covered from July 2025.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on July 1, 2024. Consent is required for sensitive data, consumers may request a list of specific third parties that received their personal data, and data protection assessments are required for higher-risk processing.

name: Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Montana residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Applicability thresholds are among the lowest in the country and were lowered further by 2025 amendments.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on October 1, 2024. Consent is required for sensitive data and for processing known minors' data for targeted advertising or sale, and data protection assessments are required for higher-risk processing.

name: Florida Digital Bill of Rights
scopeSummary: Applies to Florida residents' personal data held by covered controllers; separate provisions on sale of sensitive data, children's protections and government-directed content moderation apply more broadly.
keyObligationsSummary: Covered controllers must provide notice, honor rights to access, correct, delete and obtain a portable copy, and offer opt-outs for targeted advertising, sale and certain profiling. Consent is required for sensitive data, and additional duties apply to processing of known minors' data. The law also restricts the sale of sensitive data without notice and includes surveillance-device and voice-recognition provisions applying beyond the main revenue threshold.

name: Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act
issuingBody: Delaware General Assembly; Delaware Department of Justice
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Delaware residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Nonprofits are largely covered, with narrow exceptions.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on January 1, 2025. Consent is required for sensitive data and for targeted advertising or sale involving consumers aged 13 to 17, consumers may request a list of third-party categories, and data protection assessments are required for higher-risk processing.

name: Iowa Consumer Data Protection Act
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Iowa residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. This is among the least prescriptive comprehensive state privacy laws.
keyObligationsSummary: Requires a privacy notice and support for consumer rights to access, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, plus opt-outs where applicable for targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling. Sensitive data handling and data protection assessments follow the statute's specific rules. Controllers must use processor contracts with defined duties, and the law took effect on January 1, 2025. There is no right to correct and no data protection assessment requirement; sensitive data requires notice and an opportunity to opt out rather than opt-in consent.

name: Nebraska Data Privacy Act
scopeSummary: Applies to personal data of Nebraska residents acting in an individual or household context; employee and business-to-business contact data are generally excluded, and entity- or data-level exemptions typically cover HIPAA, GLBA and FCRA data. Applicability is based on business size rather than consumer counts.
